text:
For many of the projects I work on I found myself wanting to use a relational language like Datalog to generate C source from specifications, do verification during build or maintain a task database.

However pulling a full blown Souffle or SWI-PL as a build dependency is always a PITA and also an overkill.

So I (with the help of Claude) built awklog, a pure POSIX awk based interpreter. Copy it to your project and use during build stage or test stage with no extra dependencies.

It's a semi-naive interpreter, so decently fast, and certainly fast enough for anything you might need to do as a dev tool.

One cool usecase in particular I've been a heavy user of is a task system maintained directly in the project git repo. Just create a text file with tuples describing your tasks, their states, dependencies, hypotheses and so on. AWKLog will be able to query it for you, even recursively, and provide instant answers. Easy for AI agents to query too and no remote infrastructure dependencies at all. Everything stays in GIT, version controlled.

I hope other people will find this tool useful too.
title: Show HN: AWKLog – a minimalist Datalog interpreter in Awk

text:
Hi HN. I'm a software engineer, building Misata Studio.

Pepperwind Trading Co, is a fictional spice and tea trader from Kochi, selling in India, Europe and the US for three years. It has a storefront, a subscription club, a warehouse, ledgers in 3 currencies, support, CRM, marketing, product analytics, HR, payroll and company mail. It is around 223 tables, 79 M rows that is around 7GB of parquet files. It was made with the help of the backend engine behind misata studio.

What I found while I was researching about the synthetic dataset needs was that products that is being built for interconnected systems or analytical solutions that serve organisations often lack a real usable test dataset that is realistic enough to verify the performance and workflows accurately. And most of the time synthetic datasets don't care about entity resolution, same customers existing in different places and in different IDs, FKs pointing at rows that doesnt exist, the values might not match exactly and this is a mess when it comes to finances of the datasets. There are plenty out there, but a single heavy and massive dataset is rare. It was from a similar pain that the idea behind building misata was born.

Some things I was focussed on while building Pepperwind was for it to have unique and valuable usability for different usecases, like: - The books balance in the ledger. - 20 incidents planted in. Courier failure in Diwali, Dutch VAT charged on EU invoices, a referral fraud, price rise that pushes subscription churn etc. I made these incidents consistent across the systems. - It ships with 92 KPIs and their values each month, along with 420 questions that can be asked against the dataset.

Misata is a from scratch multi-table synthetic data generation project with an open-source python library and a web tool I am developing for prompt to dataset generation. I had posted about this in December and have come a long way since then https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46289055.

The page lets you explore a small slice of the dataset in your browser and you can follow a single customer through every system. The preview is free and the full version is paid for now, to cover the building cost ($30). Listed in huggingface under CC by 4.0 license: https://huggingface.co/datasets/misatadata/pepperwind .

I would like to reach out to people across dozens of use cases. What would you use it for and how could this or another dataset similar to this help you build your product/solution?

text:
Hey HN Community!

I created `echoChain` to explore the following phenomenon: how much data retained after LLMs exchange responses multiple times?

Imagine the game of telephone but with AIs. Each model converts the response into a question, which is then answered. After several rounds, facts get mutated, details get stripped, and the answer is far removed from the initial one.

`echoChain` is an OSS Python CLI that helps measure this process. It allows for multi-model testing, model rotation, tracking of factual claims, semantic similarity calculations, fidelity scores, reproducibility, statical tests, and visualizations. You can test models against each other, try various configurations, and learn which ones retain the most information. Right now, it only support OpenRouter; so, for this reason, please, make sure you set `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` before running it.

I wonder about the implications of these results for multi-agent systems, where AI-created information flows between agents without any human validation.

Looking forward to hearing your feedback on LLM agent building and evaluation frameworks!
title: Show HN: EchoChain to see what happens when LLMs play telephone

text:
I built an alternative to popular social networks because I was sick of the unending enshittification of instagram. Every UX change in recent years intended to make their app more addictive to teenagers has made me want to use it less, but I don't want to lose contact with the actual people that are close to me. First it was stories to make it your job to open the app every day, and then "everything is a reel" to try to get you to scroll infinitely.

This app is a more minimalist way to share photos and short videos with people you actually know. There are no public profiles so no follows, only mutuals. The feed is in reverse chronological order and there are no suggested posts or suggested connections. When sharing, you can choose the audience (you can create groups or select individual people), it's not necessarily to all your mutuals.

Other UX niceties I added are the fact that you can only see comments on your friends' posts from people you know (so no more terrible takes from their random uncle you've never met). There is also the concept of albums where the audience is the album members, who are not necessarily connected to each other, which can be useful for events or group trips.

Beyond the worsening UX of other apps, I know a lot of people who have left social media, either by deleting their account or by just never interacting, because they don't trust big tech companies with their media. E.g. people who don't share photos of their family on facebook even to only their friends. The end-to-end encryption part of the app is there for those people as well. What you share is encrypted with post-quantum keys and only the people you share a post with have the keys to decrypt it on their phone. Someone with access to the database cannot see media, captions, comments, display names, profile photos, and album and group names.

The app will never show ads since I believe that that's what drives a lot of the UX decisions on the other platforms.

It's available on both android and ios currently in Singapore, Japan, New Zealand, USA, and Canada, because those had a relatively low barrier to entry, but if there is interest I will add other countries eventually. In particular, EU countries require a legal representative there that it doesn't make sense for me to pay for right now.

text:
Small Python (spy) is a small, embeddable Python engine written in C11. Pretty much like quickjs for javascript, it's for Python.

The entire Python core language features is full implemented with almost all builtins. No Lib/ is included except sys/gc that changes the interpreter behaviors.

Is missing Python stdlib a pain? Probably no. Host injected modules allows any language's ecosystem to be used in Python syntax. Check examples, you can build game by using Raylib, or build web server using Axum/Serde_python (using Rust crates).

Just copy `spy.h`, `spyc-*.c` into your project and use it as a C library. Or several bindings are provided for languages like Js, Python, Rust, Go. You can install via pip, npm, crate, go. Worker mode is recommended so that any issue would be contained in a subprocess.

It's fast. Well, not at the speed of Pypy because it's not JIT. But it's slightly faster than C Python in most benched cases.

Another good feature is compiling Python into a binary. You could use PyInstaller, but it's gonna be so large. Small Python's binary is small. A raylib + spy based PONG game is built at around 2MB.

It's using a full suite of tests: unittest, fuzz, sanitize, bench, TLA+ specs. Despite using C, agents are unable to spot a single segfault as of now. So that's pretty cool. :)

The roadmap aims to build it for agents: snapshot/resume between durable sessions, policy declaration so agents never shoot on your feet, etc.

It has been built for one week. I have a long Claude Code session running over several days with /remote-control using Opus 5.5.

text:
I'm struggling and I hope this message gets some traction.

Are we Platform Engineers / DevOps Engineers done for?

I've been in "Platform Engineering" since it was "Unix Admin", popping Dells and Sun boxes into racks and managing full automation to bring them up to some flavor of server, to 'Systems Engineer' where you write Perl or Java code for a Fortune 50 for some product you integrated to 'DevOps Engineer' where you write terraform and manage EKS to 'Platform Engineering' where you do all those things (minus datacenter), but also are an SRE, a pipeline expert, and a 'software engineer'.

Now, companies are looking for a unicorn and there doesn't appear to be job mobility, you are either getting huge 4-500k offers for Head of roles or nothing at all. Managers are expected to be 100% hands-on, have majored in math or comp-sci, and still have the same preparation as an IC.

text:
A few days ago, I got OpenAI's email that Prism will be officially shutting down on January 1. Having written my last paper in it, I was quite disappointed since I've never really enjoyed typing LaTeX by hand for long periods. Also, when I updated my macOS recently, I started playing around with Apple's Foundation Models a bit (which I'm late on). So on Saturday I decided that, instead of studying for my midterms, my weekend project was going to be building a local version of Prism that used on-device Apple FMs.

It's an Overleaf-style editor with a PDF preview that compiles with TeX Live, and it installs TeX for you if you don't have it. To use the AI features, select text and press Cmd-K, and you can accept or reject the diff. If you have a handwritten formula that you want to insert, you can place your cursor where you want to insert and drop in a photo, which GLM-OCR turns into LaTeX locally since Apple's OCR doesn't handle math.

What was fun was testing out the capability of the models. Corollary uses SystemLanguageModel.default, which is Apple's general-purpose on-device model and the one built into macOS for Apple Intelligence. It's about 3B params with a 4,096 token context window on my M1 Max. When asked for plain text, it kept every \cite, \ref, \label and formula intact in 78 of 80 edits, but with structured output (@Generable) it went 0 for 20 because the JSON escaping eats the backslashes (\text comes back as a tab). While this limits capabilities like full document edits, you can already point it at Ollama or your own API key, and I'm sure the models will catch up soon.

Also, it needs an Apple silicon Mac, and the AI needs macOS 26 with Apple Intelligence. At this stage I don't have an Apple Developer ID yet, so the first launch needs System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway. Sorry about that. Please give it a try and let me know what bugs you run into or what the model struggles on!

Github: https://github.com/calvinyz/corollary

text:
Hi HN! We built nonce, an open-source tool that sits between personal AI agents (Muse, Grok, ChatGPT, Claude) and your personal data in Gmail, Calendar, Drive and more.

Today, if you connect Gmail to an AI agent like Muse, it can read your entire inbox. Whether on purpose or not, they can read far more emails than needed. This poses a huge data-privilege risk, in which personal data is accessed without limits.

With nonce, the AI will no longer hold your Google or Slack tokens. To read anything, it has to show its intent first:

User's question: When does my flight to Tokyo leave? Agent's justification: Need the airline confirmation email Agent's search query: from:united.com Tokyo Access needed: 10 minutes

If the justification and search query are reasonable, nonce issues a scoped token to the AI Agent. AI Agent can only query data using a token.

If something looks fishy, i.e the AI is acting on its own, wants too much, or wants sensitive emails like bank statements, medical results, or password resets. nonce sends you a notification to approve or deny.

By default, nonce denies massive crawling behaviors

How it works 1. nonce scores each search against your original question before running it, to ensure its relevance. 2. Every search is combined with the token's search. If the AI searches "bank statement", nonce runs (from:united.com Tokyo) AND (bank statement). It can narrow its access, but not widen it. 3. The token is scoped to that agent only, with a TTL for X minutes.

Limitations: nonce can't see your chat with the AI, so it can't prove you asked, which leaves a risk that the AI Agent can fake the intent. However, users can audit past accesses in nonce portal and identify these bypasses.

Give it a shot at https://github.com/roe-ai/nonce We'd love to hear what you think.

Website: https://anonce.io

text:
I usually have many projects and terminals I’m working in so Crosswalk groups my work together and allows me to open a terminal (or another terminal app) in the correct folder/project quickly and label the tab (as well as add notes). I started on iTerm2 (which is great) years ago for my terminal manager, then found I spent too much time flipping between tabs once I started leveraging terminal agents like Claude Code and Codex so I built Crosswalk to improve visibility at a glance. It originally started as a web page, but then I moved it to an app so I had better control over notifications and sounds to let me know when work was done or needed me on one of the tabs.

Crosswalk shows which sessions are still working or sitting idle with an activity dot on the tab. It provides hotkeys to jump between tabs and groups quickly. Even if you're not using agents, you can still use it for your terminal work - I commonly leave active projects as groups on the left even if I not working in them right now. There's an MCP server so an agent can launch new tabs (and agents) - it's helpful when you need a lead agent to spawn long running agents (in visible tabs) and then monitor their status (running, stuck, needs user feedback) or compact their context at efficient times. There are other nice features like layouts to view multiple terminals at once and reopens terminals from last session. I spent a bunch of time iterating on the pty host (pseudoterminal host) so updating the app or closing and then reopening will restore the sessions.

This is a paid product you can trial for free. I created it to solve the multi agent bottlenecks so I use it daily, both personally and professionally. For Mac and Windows - Electron based.

text:
In the past few weeks I've beeing working with frontier AI - Opus 5.5, Astra, Sol 6.1, Fable 5.1 and Gemini Argon.

AI has become really good at coding in some sense, that's undeniable, and there are people that say you don't really need to review their code anymore.

But I keep getting stuck in a sensation that's between cognitive dissonance, FOMO, and a vague sense of being gaslit, because when I review the code it writes - and this is all of them - 80% of it is right, and 20% is wrong, but in extremely subtle ways; only when you deeply understand the system and carefully review it do you spot the issues. These are not stylistic choices, the code is incorrect. Of course, the AI fixes it when you prompt it to, but you need to work very hard to know what needs prompting.

This is all after the grill-me skills and cross-model adversarial review and whatnot (all these techniques do help somewhat but they didn't get it perfect),

For example, I had AI (Opus 5.5 and Gemini both tried, in this particular case) write an integration test for our system, to reproduce an issue we had. It failed because it chose, for simplicity, to combine two backend fakes into one store, having writes covered by the same mutex, but the bug was only happening in production when these two stores went out of sync (and they did because we wrote to both concurrently and one write failed). (I don't want to argue the merits of the design. This is existing code.)

The wrong code it wrote to try and find the issue was carefully written, well organized, function names were reasonable, etc. etc.

I can't be alone in this, but I can't put my finger on what exactly goes wrong in the process.

Can you share examples of changes you wanted to make that Claude and the bunch (frontier versions) got subtly wrong?
title: Ask HN: What mistakes did AI make in your codebase?

text:
I spent the weekend with Claude assembling some pages for interactive exploration of a variety of basic DSP topics.

I have published the pages at https://dsp.gundy.dev/

My main goal, initially, was to build something for myself, as a way to refresh my memory and/or satisfy my curiosity on topics I love. My problem is that I find signal processing textbooks dry. Static diagrams and heavy math don't engage me very well, and I much prefer things I can interact with. As the pages started taking shape, I started thinking others might get some benefit too.

I've tried to keep the pages relatively light on math, except where it genuinely illuminates, and also keep the pages full of interactive examples. For example an in-browser acoustic modem is built up piece-by-piece and used to demonstrate modulation; multiple synths are playable with MIDI keyboards; many pages give you the ability to record your own samples and use them eg. for pitch shifting or compression or modelling your own guitar body in the physical modelling page. There's the ability to measure the SNR of your own room to determine its capacity to carry information, and much more.

I'm genuinely interested in any and all feedback - things that I could have covered better, other topics to include etc. I still have a roadmap of a number of things I'd like to cover, and I figured before I get too much deeper, it could benefit from some wider socialisation and feedback.

Also note: this is an ad-free hobby project and for the foreseeable future will remain that way.

All demos run in the browser only, no data is sent to, or processed by anything other than your own machine.

text:
Well, I have recently been attempting to gather some public Instagram data, and I must say, it is quite difficult.
Initially, I believed the process to be quite simple - obtain the data needed and done. However, it wasn't quite like this, as various issues began to arise.
A few attempts later, I got tired of dealing with the same issues repeatedly.
Afterwards, I stumbled upon API tools and attempted using many of them, they gave me free credits to test but all of them failed in json requests. But I didnt gave up and came to service named HikerApi (I didnt remember how I found it). At first I didnt expect that this service would work. They gave me 100 free requests to test in my script and it really worked! It is much simpler to use than I expected it to be. No restrictions and very fast. Also if you want to buy more requests they offer very good price ($0.001 per request). It is not an advertising, simply I want  to save your time if you want to work with scraping and gathering information on instagram I would really recommend this service.
Overall, I am learning, but at least it is not just about resolving the same issues repeatedly anymore.

Ran into this while swapping external drives between Windows and Mac -- it seems the only reliable way to keep the benefits of NTFS (journaling) and allow writes from MacOS is to use third-party $ commercial drivers.

I am not knowledgeble about what makes a driver so I asked (Gemini) -- and I am told this involves a fairly complex low level OS hooks and bypassing OS protections etc with a lot of edge cases -- so today's frontier models are unlikely to produce a reliable driver implementation.

I was surprised to hear. If we believe the AI marketing shouldn't this be solved relatively easily?
